title: The Most Excellent Way: Love
summary: Paul sets love at the center of the church's life. Without love, even tongues, prophecy, knowledge, mountain-moving faith, and total self-sacrifice amount to nothing. He describes what love does and refuses to do, and then contrasts love, which never fails, with the gifts, which are partial and will pass away when the perfect comes. Faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest is love.
story: This chapter is often read alone at weddings, but it stands in the middle of Paul's argument about spiritual gifts (chapters 12 to 14). Chapter 12 ended, “And now I will show you the most excellent way.” Chapter 14 will begin, “Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts.” Between them, Paul explains that the gifts the Corinthians prized are worthless unless they are exercised in love. Nearly every quality of love he lists answers a specific failing of the Corinthian church described earlier in the letter: they were envious and quarrelsome (3:3), boastful and puffed up (4:6, 5:2), rude at the Lord's table (11:21-22), and self-seeking in their freedom (10:24). The portrait of love is also a mirror held up to them.
historical:
Paul wrote this chapter around AD 53 to 55 to a church that valued knowledge, eloquence, and spiritual experience and was divided by status and rivalry. Greek writers had long praised love; Plato's Symposium, for example, is a dialogue in praise of eros, desire and longing for the beautiful. Paul's praise is of a different kind. He uses agape, a word that was relatively uncommon in classical Greek but had become the usual word for love in the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), including God's love for his people and the command to love God and neighbor.

Verse 3 has a textual question. Some ancient manuscripts read if I hand over my body so that I may boast, which the Berean Standard Bible reflects (“exult in the surrender of my body”), while others read so that I may be burned, the reading behind many older English versions. The Greek words differ by a single letter. The best early manuscripts favor the first reading, but on either one Paul is imagining the most extreme self-giving, done without love.
cultural:
Corinth was famous in the ancient world for its bronze, so the “ringing gong” and “clanging cymbal” (verse 1) would have sounded familiar. Cymbals and gongs were used in pagan worship, notably in the rites of Cybele and Dionysus, where loud noise accompanied ecstatic worship. Paul suggests that tongues without love are no more than that kind of religious noise.

Ancient mirrors were made of polished metal, often bronze. They gave a real but imperfect image, dimmer and less clear than modern glass mirrors. Paul's “dim reflection as in a mirror” (verse 12) uses a Greek phrase, literally in a riddle, that may also echo Numbers 12:8, where God speaks with Moses face to face and not in riddles. Adults in the ancient world also thought of childhood as a stage of incomplete reasoning to be left behind; Paul uses that picture for the partial knowledge of the present age (verse 11).
literary: The chapter is written in a lyrical, elevated prose that approaches poetry, and it has three movements. Verses 1 to 3 build a sequence of conditions, each ending in a devastating conclusion: a gong, nothing, no gain. Verses 4 to 7 describe love through fifteen verbs: two positive at the start, eight negatives, a positive contrast (it rejoices in the truth), and a final burst of four “all things” clauses. Love is personified; it acts. Verses 8 to 13 contrast the permanent and the passing, using the pairs now and then, part and whole, child and adult, mirror and face. The closing triad of faith, hope, and love appears elsewhere in Paul (1 Thessalonians 1:3; Colossians 1:4-5), suggesting a familiar early Christian summary.

outline.t: Without love, gifts and sacrifice are nothing
Love never fails; the gifts are partial
Faith, hope, and love; the greatest is love

doctrines.note: Love in this chapter is described in terms that echo God's own character in the Old Testament: patient, kind, faithful, enduring. John will later write that God is love (1 John 4:8). Christian love is a sharing in the way God himself acts toward his people.

The present is partial: we know in part and see in a dim reflection. The future brings seeing “face to face” and knowing fully, “even as I am fully known” (verse 12). Christian hope is not only for rescue but for complete knowledge of God and complete love.

Faith, hope, and love remain (verse 13). Faith is essential, yet even “absolute faith so as to move mountains” without love is nothing (verse 2). Love is the greatest because it is the life of the age to come, when faith gives way to sight.

words.note: Agape, love. Used nine times here. In the New Testament it describes God's self-giving love and the love believers are to show one another. The popular claim that agape always means a unique divine love, distinct from other Greek words for love, overstates the case, since the meaning comes from context. Here the context defines it: love is known by what it does and refuses to do.

Makrothumeo, to be patient, literally to be long-tempered, slow to anger. The Septuagint uses related words for God's patience with his people (as in Exodus 34:6, slow to anger). Love begins with patience toward others' faults, the opposite of the Corinthians' quick quarrels.

Teleios, complete, mature, perfect. “When the perfect comes, the partial passes away” (verse 10). Most interpreters take the perfect to be the state brought by Christ's return; some cessationists have taken it as the completed New Testament, and others as the church's maturity. The same word appears in 2:6 and 14:20 for the mature.

Esoptron, a mirror. In the ancient world a mirror was polished metal, giving a real but indistinct image. Paul's point is not that present knowledge of God is false, but that it is partial and indirect compared with the face-to-face knowledge to come.

christ: Paul never names Christ in this chapter, but the love he describes is the love Christ showed. Every quality, patient, kind, not self-seeking, bearing and enduring all things, describes Jesus more completely than any other person. Elsewhere Paul says that Christ “loved me and gave Himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20) and that “Christ’s love compels us” (2 Corinthians 5:14). The chapter's future vision of seeing “face to face” points to the day when believers will see the Lord himself. Christian love is not an ideal to be achieved by effort alone but a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22) and the life of Christ reproduced in his people.
questions: Read verses 4 to 7 and put your own name in place of love. Where does the description fit, and where does it expose you?
Why do you think the Corinthians, who had so many gifts, still lacked love? What gifts or strengths can hide a lack of love today?
Paul says our present knowledge of God is partial, like a dim reflection. How should that affect the way we hold our opinions and treat those who disagree?
